title: Understanding Evidence and Asking Better Equity Questions

guidance.title: Understanding Evidence and Asking Better Equity Questions
guidance.text:
Two service routes each show an eighty-percent completion rate. Have they offered equally accessible services? We cannot answer that from the percentage alone. We need to know who was included, what completion means, and what happened before people reached the point being counted.

Understanding Evidence and Asking Better Equity Questions begins with that kind of careful attention. Evidence helps staff move beyond an impression, but a number or a personal account always answers a particular question. Using it well means understanding its value and its limits, then deciding what further information would improve the work.

The course's comparison uses eight recorded completions among ten enrolled people in each route. The arithmetic is straightforward: eight out of ten is eighty percent. The harder question is about the people who never enrolled. Were they eligible but unable to reach an entry point? Did they choose another option? We have not been given that information. Equal completion among enrolled people does not establish equal access before enrollment.

You will practice separating an observation, a possible explanation, and a decision. The recorded rates are an observation. A claim about why people did not enroll is an explanation that needs evidence. A decision about what to change must also consider purpose, alternatives, and responsibility. Keeping those distinctions clear makes an analysis more useful, not less decisive. It helps colleagues see what the recommendation rests on.

There is a workplace example too. A development report records who attended a learning opportunity but not who received usable notice or could apply. Attendance can tell a team something about participation. It cannot, by itself, tell the whole story of opportunity. A supervisor or analyst may need to examine the earlier invitation and application experience before explaining who was absent.

Personal accounts add a different kind of knowledge. In another case, a participant says an online confirmation page did not work with their technology. The report records no response. The account offers a specific question about the route and what the record means. It should not be discarded because it comes from one person, or expanded into the explanation for every missing response. Its contribution is valuable at the scope it actually describes.

The course will help you ask what a number is a share of, whether definitions and periods match, and whose experience may be missing. You will consider why an overall result can hide different experiences and why a before-and-after change does not prove its own cause. Culture briefs and community knowledge can widen the questions, while direct evidence is still needed to examine them.

Your final practice is a short evidence note in plain language. It should explain what is known, what remains uncertain, and which next question matters to the decision. That skill is useful when reviewing service access, staff opportunities, a policy proposal, or a report for leadership. You do not have to make the evidence say more than it does. A careful account can give people a stronger basis for deciding what to examine and what to do next.

Try the evidence note this way: “Both routes recorded eight completions among ten enrolled people. We do not know who tried to enroll or whether the entry route worked for them. Before recommending a change, examine the invitation and enrollment experience alongside the completion record.” The note keeps the useful finding and gives a specific next inquiry. It neither declares equal access nor assumes a barrier occurred. That is the distinction you will practice.

guidance.title: The people inside and outside the percentage
guidance.text: Eight completions out of ten enrolled people describes those ten people. It tells us nothing yet about how many tried to enroll or could not reach the route. Keep the eighty-percent result; it is useful for its actual question. Then name the question outside it. That is how a sound calculation can become a more useful equity inquiry.
